 "identityCheck": "The title Sport-Related Injury and Performance Enhancing Substance Use by Young Athletes matches the filename, and the article's own DOI 10.1177/19417381241287199 is printed on page 1.",
 "confidence": "high",
 "studyDesign": "Cross-sectional Study",
 "primaryDomain": "Athlete Wellbeing",
 "domains": ["Athlete Wellbeing", "Sports Medicine & Injury", "Nutrition & Hydration"],
 "audiences": ["Sports Medicine", "Athletic Training", "Coaching"],
 "sports": ["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations": ["Youth / Adolescent", "Male Athletes", "Female Athletes", "Injured Athletes", "Healthy Athletes"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Cross-sectional analysis of 952 athletes aged 6 to 25 years (mean age 14, 56% female) who attended an injury prevention evaluation at a tertiary pediatric center from 2013 to 2020. Legal performance enhancing substance (PES) use was reported by 14% and consideration of banned PES use by 3%; unadjusted, season-ending injury was linked to legal PES use (OR 2.74), but after adjustment injury group was not associated with either outcome.",
 "screeningLimitations": "Self-reported questionnaire data from an injury prevention clinic, in a largely white and middle-to-upper income sample, so it is not representative. The cross-sectional design cannot establish whether injury preceded PES use, and only three athletes reported banned PES use for performance, too few for analysis.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read the unadjusted odds ratios, such as 2.74 for season-ending injury and legal PES use, as evidence that injury drives supplement use, when the adjusted models show no association with injury and the design cannot show direction.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2024,
  "citation": "McNaughton M, Hunt D, Parmeter B, O'Brien M, Cook D, Meehan W, et al. Sport-Related Injury and Performance Enhancing Substance Use by Young Athletes. Sports Health. 2024.",
  "doi": "10.1177/19417381241287199",
  "abstract": "Compares legal performance enhancing substance (PES) use and consideration of banned PES use in young athletes aged 6 to 25 with a season-ending injury, concussion, non-season-ending injury or no injury, using a cross-sectional dataset from 2013 to 2020. The authors found no association between injury group and PES use after adjustment, and identify male sex, depression history, weight training and belief that weight affects ability as factors linked to PES use.",
  "tldr": "Among young athletes at an injury prevention clinic, 14% reported legal PES use and 3% considered banned PES. Injury status was not associated with either after adjustment; male sex, depression history, weight training and belief that weight affects ability were.",
  "methods": "Cross-sectional analysis of an existing dataset from an injury prevention evaluation (April 2013 to March 2020). Athletes completed an electronic questionnaire covering PES use, injury history, sport contact level and other factors. Multivariable logistic regression used injury group as the exposure, with unadjusted and adjusted models.",
  "findings": "Of 952 athletes, 133 had a season-ending injury, 441 a non-season-ending injury, 85 a concussion and 293 no injury. Legal PES use was reported by 136 (14%) and consideration of banned PES use by 28 (3%). Unadjusted, season-ending injury versus no injury gave OR 2.74 for legal PES use and OR 4.01 (95% CI 1.15 to 13.96) for banned PES consideration. In the adjusted models, injury groups were not associated with legal PES use (season-ending injury OR 1.00, 95% CI 0.51 to 1.95). Male sex (OR 1.38), depression history (OR 3.01), weight training (OR 1.66) and belief that weight affects athletic ability (OR 1.75) were associated with legal PES use. Older age (OR 1.18) and male sex (OR 1.57) were associated with banned PES consideration.",
  "limitations": "Self-report may under-report PES use, and the authors could not determine whether PES use began before or after injury. The sample is one clinic's population with a wide age range and regional limits. The abstract's statement of no association refers to adjusted models; the unadjusted injury associations were significant. The text gives 954 athletes after exclusions while the tables use 952. The questionnaire offered only male or female sex options when it was designed.",
  "practicalImplications": "When seeing young athletes for injury prevention, ask about legal supplement use and weight-related beliefs, and give extra attention to the male, depression and weight-training flags reported here. Do not assume that an injured young athlete is more likely to use PES, because the adjusted analysis did not show this.",
  "athleteDev": "Performance Application: For young athletes who weight train or believe weight affects performance, coaches and clinicians can review supplement use and education needs. The study does not show that these practices improve performance or safety.",
  "rtp": "Return to Sport Application: The study does not support a PES-based change to return-to-play care, because injury status was not associated with PES use after adjustment. It cannot show whether PES use affects recovery."
 }
}

                                      PES use. This study examines legal PES use and consideration of banned PES use in young athletes with a season-ending
                                      injury (SEI) compared to young athletes with non-SEI/no previous injury.
                                      Hypothesis: Young athletes sustaining SEI or concussions have increased odds of reporting legal PES use and

                                      consideration of banned PES use. In adjusted analysis, athletes who were male (odds ratio [OR], 1.38; 95% CI, 1.16-1.73;
                                      P = 0.03), have history of depression (OR, 3.01; 95% CI, 1.26-7.18; P = 0.01), weight train (OR, 1.66; 95% CI, 1.04-2.65;
                                      P = 0.03), and believe that athletic ability is influenced by weight (OR, 1.75; 95% CI, 1.08-2.83; P = 0.02) had increased odds
                                      of reporting legal PES use. Older (OR, 1.18; 95% CI, 1.03-1.36; P = 0.02) and male (OR, 1.57; 95% CI, 1.02-1.81; P < 0.04)
                                      athletes had increased odds of consideration of banned PES use.

                                      concussion regardless of injury type or severity. Factors associated with PES use were male sex, age, history of depression,
                                      weight training, and belief that weight affects athletic performance.

     of athletic injury. We acknowledge that PES use in different
     contact-sport athletes may be impacted by individual sport type
     and culture, regional PES education level among athletes, and
     societal standards.
       There are several limitations to our study to consider. The data
     were self-reported, and as such, responses may not be truthful,
     as athletes may be reluctant to report PES use for fear of getting
     in trouble or social stigma. For the athletes who reported PES
     use, we were unable to ascertain whether they began using a
     legal PES or considered banned PES use before or after their
     documented injury. Consideration of banned PES use is not a
     proxy for PES use. The wide age range and regionality of the
     data set may limit the generalizability of our findings. At the

     answer. Our cohort was largely white and middle- to upper-SES

     PES patterns in young athletes exist in the literature.4,11 Finally,
     we did not stratify the athletes with SEI and non-SEI by time

  "abstract": "Combines a focused PRISMA systematic review of sport-related structural brain injury from 2012 onward with a cross-sectional survey of 31 international sports neurosurgeons on operative management and return to play.   "findings": "Of 241 records, 27 studies were included. Nine articles (12 athletes) reported return-to-play information, and 10 of those 12 cases were high school athletes or younger. Among 31 responding neurosurgeons, 12 (38.7%) would not operate on an acute, asymptomatic structural injury; midline shift over 10 mm (63.2%) and hemorrhage over 10 mm (52.6%) were the most common operative indications among those who would. For resolved hemorrhage, most experts allowed return to high-contact sport at 6 to 12 months, and about 80% did not endorse return to high-contact sport with persistent hemorrhage. After craniotomy, 40% to 50% considered return at 6 to 12 months. Linear regression found that experts allowed earlier return at higher levels of play (beta -0.58, P = .033).",
  "limitations": "The systematic review yields little (27 studies, 12 athletes with return data), and the survey reflects opinion rather than outcomes. The regression is printed as beta -0.58 with 95% CI -0.111 to -0.005, which places the point estimate outside its own interval; this inconsistency appears in both the abstract and the results and should be checked against the source. The authors also note heterogeneity in both the literature and the survey responses.",
  "practicalImplications": "Use the paper as a structured aid for individualized decisions rather than a return-to-play protocol. Note the authors' finding that experts were more lenient at higher competition levels, and that they were more conservative after craniotomy or with persistent hemorrhage.",
  "athleteDev": "Performance Application: The review does not inform training load. Its only performance-relevant point is that expert views on return timing varied with level of play, so athletes at higher competition levels need individual planning with the treating neurosurgeon.",
  "rtp": "Return to Sport Application: Use it to frame the range of expert opinion on operative indications and return timing, such as 6 to 12 months for high-contact sport after resolved hemorrhage and no return for persistent hemorrhage in about 80% of experts. It cannot replace individual neurological and imaging assessment, and the evidence base is 12 athletes plus opinion."

  "doi": "10.1123/ijsnem.2019-0300",
  "abstract": "Position of Sports Dietitians Australia that exertional heat stress challenges athletes' nutritional status, health and performance.   "tldr": "Heat stress makes hydration, fuelling and gut comfort harder, so athletes should start euhydrated, practise their drinking plan in training and acclimatize where possible. It recommends assessing fluid balance, gastrointestinal tolerance and thirst responses. Ice-slurry and cold beverages may help in hot, humid, still conditions but may not in warm, dry, windy settings, and menthol can alter thermal sensation. Table 3 gives sport-specific advice: endurance athletes should practise fluid plans in training and keep carbohydrate intake steady, and para-sport athletes should avoid overhydration.",
  "limitations": "The statement is a consensus document with no new data and no described grading system.   "practicalImplications": "Measure sweat losses and hydration status in training that mimics the hot event, and practise the fluid and carbohydrate plan there.   "athleteDev": "Performance Application: Heat acclimation, starting euhydrated and practised fluid and carbohydrate plans are the main performance steps. Cold beverages and menthol can improve perceived comfort, though the statement says their value depends on conditions.",
  "rtp": "Return to Sport Application: Not addressed. The statement covers hot-weather nutrition and hydration and gives no guidance on return after illness or injury, so it cannot inform return-to-play decisions."

     It is the position of Sports Dietitians Australia (SDA) that exercise in hot and/or humid environments, or with signiﬁcant clothing
     and/or equipment that prevents body heat loss (i.e., exertional heat stress), provides signiﬁcant challenges to an athlete’s nutritional
     status, health, and performance. Exertional heat stress, especially when prolonged, can perturb thermoregulatory, cardiovascular,
     and gastrointestinal systems. Heat acclimation or acclimatization provides beneﬁcial adaptations and should be undertaken where
     possible. Athletes should aim to begin exercise euhydrated. Furthermore, preexercise hyperhydration may be desirable in some
     scenarios and can be achieved through acute sodium or glycerol loading protocols. The assessment of ﬂuid balance during exercise,
     together with gastrointestinal tolerance to ﬂuid intake, and the appropriateness of thirst responses provide valuable information
     to inform ﬂuid replacement strategies that should be integrated with event fuel requirements. Such strategies should also consider
     ﬂuid availability and opportunities to drink, to prevent signiﬁcant under- or overconsumption during exercise. Postexercise beverage
     choices can be inﬂuenced by the required timeframe for return to euhydration and co-ingestion of meals and snacks. Ingested
     beverage temperature can inﬂuence core temperature, with cold/icy beverages of potential use before and during exertional heat
     stress, while use of menthol can alter thermal sensation. Practical challenges in supporting athletes in teams and traveling for
     competition require careful planning. Finally, speciﬁc athletic population groups have unique nutritional needs in the context of
     exertional heat stress (i.e., youth, endurance/ultra-endurance athletes, and para-sport athletes), and speciﬁc adjustments to nutrition
     strategies should be made for these population groups.

      To test this new concept, we recently conducted a pilot
   study in well-trained Kenyan athletes to investigate the ef-
   fects of alginate hydrogel as a unique fluid and CHO de-
   livery system. A secondary aim was to determine the loss in
   body mass in well-trained Kenyan runners drinking ad
   libitum during strenuous exercise conducted at moderate
   altitude (approximately 2000 m above sea level) to estimate
   the levels of dehydration. For this pilot study, 16 well-
   trained Kenyan runners provided written consent to be part
   of the study and provided near nude body mass before and
   after the training runs. The average body mass before the
   run was 54.0 T 3.9 kg. The training run was 25.1 km, with
   an average temperature of 20.1-C and relative humidity of
   37%. The average pace was 3:48 minIkmj1 and the run was
   completed within 95 min; the change in altitude during the
   run was approximately 500 m. A CHO drink containing
   approximately 40 to 50 gILj1 CHO was provided to all
   athletes every 5 km in sufficient volume to allow drinking ad
   libitum. Four athletes were provided with either 180 gILj1 or
   300 gILj1 CHO using alginate hydrogel (i.e., maltodextrin to
   fructose ratio of 1:0.7). Drinking bottles were collected fol-
   lowing each 5 km station to assess fluid consumption; the
   bottles of one athlete were damaged during the run and thus
   this data has been omitted. After the completion of the run,
   the average body mass was 51.7 T 3.7 kg, representing a
   water deficit of 4.2 T 1.0% body mass loss, with a range
   of 2.2% to 5.9%. For the three athletes using the alginate
   hydrogel drink, 291.3 T 26.4 mL was consumed over the
   95 min. While this research is ongoing, there are some en-
   couraging preliminary findings. Firstly, all athletes failed to
   prevent a decrease in body mass of e2% despite having regular
   access to sports drinks. Secondarily, there were no reports of
   any GI distress with any drink including the alginate hydrogel.

(32) (Fig. 2). The combination of maltodextrin and fructose
has repeatedly been shown to increase exogenous CHO ox-
idation compared with glucose-only ingestion up to a maxi-
mum of 1.8 gIminj1 (34).
   Current ACSM guidelines recommend the ingestion of 30
to 60 gIhj1 during prolonged endurance exercise lasting
between 1 and 2.5 h and up to 90 gIhj1 during ultra-
                                                                        
endurance exercise exceeding 2 h (35). While these recom-               
mendations are generally well accepted, there is research               
that suggests no further benefit of ingesting CHO in excess

 alginate hydrogel as high as 300 gIL-1 of CHO was well                 
tolerated, illustrating the unique ability of hydrogels to              
provide CHO in concentrations that far exceed what can                  
typically be tolerated using commercially available sports              
drinks. Although there is only indirect evidence for its er-            
gogenic effect, the winners of the 2016/2017 Berlin, Chi-               
cago, New York, Tokyo, Boston, and London marathons                     
all used a CHO beverage containing alginate hydrogel,                   
demonstrating its popularity in the elite field (43). Given its         
potential, further research is required to quantify the effect of       
alginate hydrogel on exogenous CHO oxidation and gastric                
emptying rates before the efficacy of this new delivery system          
can be confirmed. For example, the provision of a high con-             
centration of CHO during exercise using this innovation can             
easily be modified to deliver other essential substrates/nutri-         
ents that may otherwise not be so well tolerated by the GI              
tract, such as protein (40) and iron status regulating drugs
